subject: economics
prompt: Which description fits a **multinational corporation (MNC)**?

image.alt: A head office connected to factories in four different places

options.text: A company that sells goods in many countries but produces in only one
A company that owns or controls production in more than one nation
A company owned jointly by the governments of several nations
Any company that exports even a small part of its goods

hint: The key word is production, not selling.
explanation: The chapter defines an MNC as a company that **owns or controls production in more than one nation**. Selling abroad alone (option a) or exporting a little (option d) is just trade. Ownership by governments (option c) is not part of the definition.

subject: economics
prompt: Until the middle of the twentieth century, production was largely organised **within** countries. What did colonies such as India do in trade at that time?

image.alt: Ships carrying raw materials out of a colony and finished goods back in

options.text: Exported raw materials and food stuff and imported finished goods
Exported finished goods and imported raw materials
Exported machines and imported food stuff
Did not trade at all because MNCs controlled everything

hint: Think of what a colony sent out and what it got back.
explanation: Colonies such as India **exported raw materials and food stuff and imported finished goods**, and **trade** was the main channel connecting distant countries. MNCs had not yet emerged, so option (d) is wrong, and option (b) reverses the pattern.

subject: economics
prompt: A large MNC would spend ₹2,000 crore on producing a batch of goods in one country. The chapter says spreading production across borders can mean **50-60 per cent cost-savings**. Between what amounts would the savings lie?

image.alt: Two bars of cost: 100 units in one country and 40 to 50 units when production is spread

options.text: ₹800 crore to ₹1,000 crore
₹100 crore to ₹120 crore
₹1,000 crore to ₹1,200 crore
₹50 crore to ₹60 crore

hint: Find 50 per cent and 60 per cent of the cost, not of 100.
explanation: 50 per cent of ₹2,000 crore is ₹1,000 crore and 60 per cent is ₹1,200 crore, so the **saving** is ₹1,000 to ₹1,200 crore. The traps: ₹800 to ₹1000 crore is what the MNC would **still pay** (cost after saving); ₹100 to ₹120 crore uses 5 and 6 per cent; ₹50 to ₹60 crore treats the percentages as crores.

subject: economics
prompt: The money spent to buy assets such as land, buildings, machines and equipment is called **investment**. Which picture shows **foreign investment** by an MNC?

image.alt: Five stages of an MNC's production in different places

options.text: A shop

image.alt: A shop

options.text: Trade

image.alt: A ship carrying goods between two countries

options.text: People

image.alt: People travelling with bags

options.text: Factory

image.alt: A foreign company building a factory with a crane

hint: Which picture has an MNC spending money on assets in another country?
explanation: Foreign investment is investment made by MNCs, for example in a **new factory** built in another country. The ship shows **foreign trade**, the travellers show **movement of people**, and the shop is just a place to buy goods. All the investment is made in the hope that the assets will earn profits.

subject: economics
prompt: Some MNCs set up production **jointly with local companies**. What is the two-fold benefit to the local company?

image.alt: An MNC sending money and technology to a local company

options.text: The MNC provides money for additional investment, such as new machines, and may bring the latest technology
The MNC pays all the local company's taxes and gives it cheaper land
The MNC closes rival firms so the local company has no competition
The MNC lowers the wages of the local company's workers

hint: One benefit is money, the other is know-how.
explanation: The chapter says joint production helps the local company in two ways: the MNC can provide **money for additional investments** (like new machines for faster production) and may bring the **latest technology**. Taxes, closing rivals and lower wages are not mentioned.

subject: economics
prompt: Cargill Foods, a large American MNC, bought over the Indian company Parakh Foods, which had a well-reputed brand, a large marketing network and four oil refineries. What does this show?

image.alt: A large MNC taking over a smaller local company

options.text: MNCs usually build all their factories from scratch
Buying up local companies and then expanding production is the most common route for MNC investments
MNCs avoid competing with local companies
Foreign investment can only take place as joint production

hint: Cargill took control of existing assets instead of building new ones.
explanation: The chapter says the **most common route** for MNC investment is to **buy up local companies and then expand production**. Wealthy MNCs can do this easily; Cargill gained control of Parakh's refineries and network and became India's largest edible oil producer. Options (a), (c) and (d) contradict this.

subject: economics
prompt: Large MNCs in developed countries place orders with a large number of small producers around the world and sell the goods under their own brand names. Which picture shows this?

image.alt: Icons for footballs and shoes, a tag, an office, a call centre and a car

options.text: Joint production

image.alt: Two companies producing together

options.text: New factory

image.alt: A new factory being built

options.text: Orders to small producers

image.alt: Many small producers sending goods to one big company

options.text: Take-over

image.alt: A large company taking over a small one

hint: Many small hands, one big brand.
explanation: Garments, footwear and sports items are examples of production by **many small producers** who supply the MNC. The MNC then sells under its own brand and has great power to decide **price, quality, delivery and labour conditions**. The other pictures show joint production, a new plant and a take-over.

subject: economics
prompt: By 2017 Ford Motors was selling 88,000 cars in the Indian market while 1,81,000 cars were exported from India. What percentage of these cars (sold in India plus exported) was **exported**?

image.alt: Bars: 88,000 sold in India, 1,81,000 exported, 2,69,000 total

hint: The denominator is the total, not either part.
explanation: Total = 88,000 + 1,81,000 = 2,69,000 cars. Exported share = 1,81,000 / 2,69,000 × 100 = **67.3%**. Traps: 32.7% is the share sold **in India**; 205.7% divides exports by home sales only; 48.6% divides home sales by exports. This also shows MNC plants produce for the Indian market and for export.

subject: economics
prompt: What does the chapter say happens when trade opens and goods travel from one country's market to another?

image.alt: Goods moving between two markets and prices coming closer

options.text: Choice of goods rises, prices of similar goods tend to become equal and producers in the two countries compete closely
Choice of goods falls and prices in the two countries move further apart
Prices become equal only because both governments fix them
Only the producers gain; buyers have fewer goods to pick from

hint: Think of Chinese toys and Indian toys in the same shop.
explanation: With the opening of trade, goods move between markets, **choice rises**, **prices of similar goods tend to become equal**, and producers compete even though thousands of miles apart. This is called the **integration of markets**. Prices are not fixed by governments (c), and buyers gain choice (d).

subject: economics
prompt: Which statement best describes **globalisation** as used in the chapter?

image.alt: Links between countries: goods and services, investment, technology, people

options.text: The spread of one country's culture to the rest of the world
A country producing everything it needs without trade
The movement of people between countries in search of jobs
The process of rapid integration or interconnection between countries through foreign trade and foreign investment

hint: The chapter ties it to trade and investment by MNCs.
explanation: The chapter describes globalisation as the **rapid integration or interconnection between countries**, brought about by greater **foreign trade and foreign investment**, with MNCs playing a major role. Movement of people has not increased much because of restrictions, so (c) is not the main meaning.

subject: economics
prompt: A government puts a **limit on the number of goods** that can be imported. Which picture shows this trade barrier, called a quota?

image.alt: Cards for investment, tax on imports, a limit on goods and removed barriers

options.text: Tax on imports

image.alt: Goods with a tax tag

options.text: Quota

image.alt: A gate letting only a few boxes through

options.text: Subsidy

image.alt: A government giving money to a farmer

options.text: People

image.alt: People travelling with bags

hint: A quota is about quantity, not price.
explanation: A **quota** caps the quantity of goods allowed in, like a gate that lets only a few boxes through. A **tax on imports** raises their price instead. Giving money to farmers is a **subsidy**, which is different from a trade barrier on imports.

subject: economics
prompt: Suppose the Indian government puts a **tax on imported toys**. What is the likely result?

image.alt: Two panels: no tax with many cheap toys and tax with fewer costly toys

options.text: Imported toys become cheaper and imports rise
Imports stay the same because buyers do not notice the tax
Imported toys become costlier, imports reduce and Indian toy-makers prosper
Indian toy-makers face greater competition than before

hint: Who pays the tax, and what happens to the price?
explanation: Importers must pay the tax, so buyers pay a **higher price**. Imported toys are no longer as cheap, imports **automatically reduce** and **Indian toy-makers prosper**. A tax on imports is an example of a **trade barrier**.

subject: economics
prompt: Why did India put barriers on foreign trade and foreign investment after Independence?

image.alt: Young factories protected by a dome from imports

options.text: To protect producers within the country from foreign competition, since industries were only just coming up in the 1950s and 1960s
To stop every kind of import, including machinery and fertilisers
To improve the quality of goods by exposing producers to world competition
Because the WTO had asked all countries to protect their industries

hint: New industries need time before they can face imports.
explanation: Industries were just coming up in the **1950s and 1960s**, and competition from imports would not have let them grow, so barriers were set up. India still allowed imports of **essential items such as machinery, fertilisers and petroleum** (b is wrong). Exposing producers to competition was the reason for removing barriers around 1991 (c).

subject: economics
prompt: Which statement about the **World Trade Organisation (WTO)** is correct?

image.alt: An organisation building with many member countries around it

options.text: It was started at the initiative of developing countries to protect their farmers
It allows every country to keep any trade barrier it likes
It aims to liberalise international trade, sets rules on trade and sees that they are obeyed
It was set up by India after 1991 to attract foreign companies

hint: Its name tells you the area it deals with: trade rules.
explanation: The WTO's aim is to **liberalise international trade**; it **establishes rules** regarding international trade and sees that they are obeyed. It was started at the initiative of **developed** countries and has about 160 members. In practice developed countries have unfairly kept some barriers.

subject: economics
prompt: Removing the barriers or restrictions set by the government on foreign trade and investment is called **liberalisation**. Which picture shows liberalised trade?

image.alt: Timeline with a wall, an open way, a factory and an international body

options.text: Wall

image.alt: A high wall between two sides with ships outside

options.text: Tax

image.alt: Goods with a tax tag

options.text: Quota

image.alt: A gate letting only a few boxes through

options.text: Open trade

image.alt: Open trade with goods moving both ways

hint: Liberal means with fewer restrictions.
explanation: With liberalisation, businesses decide freely what to import or export and goods move easily **both ways**. The wall, the tax and the quota are all **barriers** that restrict trade.

subject: economics
prompt: In the United States agriculture contributes **1 per cent of GDP** and **0.5 per cent of total employment**. Output per person employed in agriculture is how many times the output per person in the whole economy (GDP share divided by employment share)?

options.text: 1 time
2 times
0.5 times
1.5 times

hint: Divide the share of GDP by the share of employment.
explanation: 1% / 0.5% = **2 times**. Traps: 0.5 turns the ratio upside down; 1.5 adds the two shares; 1 assumes equal shares mean equal output per person. The chapter uses these small shares to show how few US farmers receive massive government money.

subject: economics
prompt: According to the chapter, who has benefited **most** from globalisation and greater competition in India?

image.alt: Groups that gained on the left and groups that struggled on the right

options.text: Well-off urban consumers, and producers with skill, education and wealth
All workers in the unorganised sector
Small producers of batteries, toys and tyres
Workers hired on a flexible basis

hint: The impact has not been uniform.
explanation: Greater choice, better quality and lower prices mostly helped **well-off urban consumers**, and people with **education, skill and wealth** used the new opportunities best. Small producers and flexibly hired workers often struggled.

They are the only industries allowed in rural India
These industries need no raw materials
These products and services have a large number of well-off buyers

subject: economics
prompt: How does **flexibility in labour laws** help companies, according to the chapter?

image.alt: A year of months: permanent workers all year and flexible workers in a few months

options.text: They must pay overtime at a double rate
They can hire workers for short periods when work pressure is high, which reduces labour costs
They must give all workers provident fund and health insurance
They are exempt from taxes for five years

hint: Flexible hiring means workers are not kept on all year.
explanation: Instead of hiring regular workers, companies hire workers **'flexibly' for short periods** when pressure of work is intense, which **reduces the cost of labour**. Double-rate overtime, provident fund and insurance belong to **permanent** jobs; the five-year tax holiday applies to SEZs.

subject: economics
prompt: Ravi's capacitor unit had 20 workers at its peak and now has 7 workers. By what percentage has the number of workers **fallen**?

image.alt: Bars: 20 workers after expansion and 7 workers now

hint: Fall = (old - new) divided by old.
explanation: Fall = (20 − 7) / 20 × 100 = **65%**. Traps: 35% is the share that **remains**; 13% treats the drop in workers as a percentage; 185.7% divides by the new number. The unit suffered after import restrictions on capacitors were removed in 2001 and TV companies chose imported capacitors at half the price.

subject: economics
prompt: Sushila leaves home at 7:30 a.m. and returns at 10 p.m., seven days a week. How many hours is she away from home each day?

image.alt: A 24 hour bar with the away period from 7:30 in the morning to 10 at night

options.text: 2.5 hours
14 hours
14.5 hours
15 hours

hint: Convert 10 p.m. to the 24-hour clock first.
explanation: 10 p.m. is 22:00, so 22:00 − 7:30 = **14 hours 30 minutes = 14.5 hours**. Traps: 2.5 hours subtracts 7:30 from 10 without converting p.m.; 14 hours rounds the start to 8:00; 15 hours rounds the start down to 7:00. At this rate she is away about 101.5 hours a week, with no benefits and no wage on a day off.
